core.text: A verb turned into a noun, so it can take a case or follow a preposition, is **the gerund (the '-ing' noun form: ad bibendum = for drinking)**: *tempus dormiendī* — time for sleeping; *parātus ad audiendum* — ready for listening; *fessus audiendō* — tired from listening. It is the present stem + -nd- with neuter endings. Latin name: *gerundium*.
*Running is fun*, *shoes for running*: here *running* is a noun, a gerund. In *the running man* it is a participle, an adjective.

Stem + -ndum (after ad: purpose), -ndī ('of …-ing' after a noun or adjective), -ndō (means, or after in / dē / ab). First conjugation -andum; second and third -endum; fourth, and the -iō verbs of the third, -iendum.

invented.la: Puerī ad lūdendum in hortum currunt.
invented.en: The boys run into the garden to play.

core.text: The same -nd- makes **the gerundive (the '-nd-' adjective: 'to be done'; aqua bibenda = water to be drunk)**. The gerund is a neuter noun standing alone (*ad bibendum* — for drinking); the gerundive agrees with a noun (*ad aquam bibendam* — for drinking water, *bibendum est* — one must drink). A noun to agree with means gerundive.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 26) list the uses: *ad* + accusative for purpose (*vās ad bibendum*), genitive after a noun (*tempus veniendī, ars scrībendī*) or an adjective (*studiōsus discendī*), *in* + ablative for time (*in ambulandō* — while walking), *ab / dē / ex* + ablative (*dē amandō*), and the bare ablative for means (*ambulandō* — by walking). With *causā* after a genitive it means 'for the sake of': *dēlectandī causā*.

Ørberg (cap. XXVI) declines it: *nārrandum, nārrandī, nārrandō*; a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks) forms it the same way (*loquendī*). It has no nominative — as a subject Latin uses the infinitive (*dormīre iuvat* — sleeping is pleasant) — and the dative (-ndō) is rare. A gerund with a direct object is usually replaced by the gerundive: *ad flōrēs carpendōs* rather than *ad carpendum flōrēs*.
English does the same in 'running is fun' and 'shoes for running': there *running* names the activity, it does not describe anybody.

teach.title: A verb doing a noun's job

notice.ask: Tap the word after ad that names the activity — what do the two words share?

teach.say: A verb can be turned into a noun, so that it takes a case and follows a preposition, and that noun is **the gerund (the '-ing' noun form: ad bibendum = for drinking)**. *Puerī ad lūdendum in hortum currunt* — the boys run into the garden for playing. English does the same in 'shoes for running'.

teach.title: The accusative: ad + -ndum
teach.say: Take the present stem, add *-nd-*, then a neuter ending. After *ad*, meaning 'for' or 'in order to', that ending is *-um*: *ad pugnandum*, *ad bibendum*, *ad dormiendum*. First-conjugation verbs give *-andum* (*pugnandum*); the second and third give *-endum* (*bibendum*, *lūdendum*); the fourth, and the *-iō* verbs of the third, give *-iendum* (*dormiendum*, *audiendum*, *faciendum*).

teach.title: The genitive: -ndī
teach.say: After a noun or an adjective the ending is *-ī*, the 'of' form: *ars scrībendī*, the art of writing; *discendī cupidus*, eager for learning; *docendī causā*, for the sake of teaching. English says '-ing' here too, so listen for the hidden 'of'.

teach.title: The ablative: -ndō
teach.say: The ending *-ō* says how something is done — 'by …-ing': *Multa discimus legendō et audiendō*, we learn much by reading and by listening. After *in* the same *-ō* says 'while': *in scrībendō*, while writing.

show.say: scrībendō — by writing, and after in, while writing

teach.title: The verbs that keep their i
teach.say: The fourth conjugation, and the *-iō* verbs of the third, slip an *-i-* in before the *-nd-*: *dormiendum*, *audiendum*, *faciendī*, *accipiendō*. It is the same *i* they already carry in *dormiunt*, *audiunt* and *faciunt*: if the present has it, the gerund keeps it.

show.say: dormiendum — the fourth conjugation keeps its i

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: The gerund has no nominative at all: for 'sleeping is good' Latin uses the infinitive, *dormīre bonum est*. Everywhere else the three endings carry the sense — *-ndum* after *ad*, *-ndī* after a noun or adjective, *-ndō* for how or while — and a sentence may hold two of them at once.
